title: Observation vs Interpretation
keyIdea: An observation is what you see, hear, or measure. An interpretation is a guess about why or what it means. Keep them separate so claims rest on evidence.
familyTip: Look out the window together. Ask: 'What do you see?' then 'What do you think is going on?' Label each sentence as see or think.

visual.caption: Observation or interpretation? Drag each clue, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort see/hear from guesses, name jar drops, reject angry-as-observation, match height evidence, then challenge.

kid: An observation is what you see, hear, or measure.
An interpretation is a guess about why or what it means.
"The dog barked" is what you heard. "It was angry" is a guess.
Good science claims need observations as evidence.
adult: Working scientifically (KS1/KS2): an observation is what you see, hear or measure. An interpretation is a guess about why. Words: observe, evidence, claim, measure.
Common mistakes: calling a feeling an observation; using "I feel it grew" as evidence; treating observation and interpretation as the same.
In the lab your child sorts clues, names water drops (not a homesick jar), rejects angry as an observation, and links growth to measured height.

practice.hint: Can you see or measure it?
practice.explain: Melting is what you sense — an observation.

practice.prompt: "The dog was angry" after a bark is…
practice.hint: You heard a bark; anger is a meaning you added.
practice.explain: Anger is an interpretation layered on the bark.

practice.prompt: A plant was {a} cm, now {b} cm. Growth in cm?
practice.hint: Subtract start height from new height.
practice.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a} cm — an observation used as evidence.

practice.prompt: You record {n} beeps. How many did you hear?
practice.explain: You heard {n} beeps — that count is the observation.

practice.prompt: Order steps to check a claim carefully.
items: see if the observation supports the guess
practice.explain: Separate observation from interpretation, then test the link.

pool.hint: Ask what your eyes actually saw on the glass.
pool.explain: Drops are sensed; sadness is a story.

pool.hint: Prefer a number you measured with a ruler.
pool.explain: Measured height change is observation evidence.

pool.prompt: Which can you check by looking?
pool.hint: Colour is something you can see and check.
pool.explain: Green is checkable; jealousy is not.
Keep them distinct so claims rest on evidence.

pool.prompt: Thermometer shows {t} °C. What temperature did you observe?
pool.hint: Read the number shown on the instrument.
pool.explain: {t} °C is the observation from the thermometer.

pool.prompt: Count {a} red blocks and {b} blue. How many blocks observed in all?
pool.hint: Add the red and blue counts you can see.

choices: so claims rest on what was sensed
pool.explain: Guesses are fine when labelled; claims need observations.

pool.prompt: Order: talk about a dog bark carefully.
items: say your guess (maybe it wants food)
keep the guess labelled as a guess
pool.hint: Start from the sense data you heard.
pool.explain: Report the bark, then the guess, clearly separated.
